danish.title: Ellevte bog (1812) — Kapitel 34
paragraphs: Efter at have løbet gennem forskellige gårde og sidegader nåede Pierre med sin lille byrde tilbage til Gruzínskij-haven på hjørnet af Povarskój. Han genkendte i første omgang ikke stedet, hvorfra han var gået ud for at lede efter barnet, så overfyldt var det nu med mennesker og ejendele, der var slæbt ud af husene. Foruden russiske familier, der havde søgt tilflugt her fra branden med deres ejendele, var der adskillige franske soldater i forskelligt tøj. Pierre lagde ikke mærke til dem. Han skyndte sig at finde embedsmandens familie for at give datteren tilbage til moderen og så gå hen og redde en anden. Pierre følte, at han stadig havde meget at gøre, og det hurtigt. Glødende af varmen og af at have løbet følte han i det øjeblik stærkere end nogensinde den ungdommelighed, livfuldhed og beslutsomhed, der havde grebet ham, da han løb for at redde barnet. Hun var nu blevet rolig og klyngede sig med sine små hænder til Pierres frakke og sad på hans arm og kiggede sig omkring som et lille vildt dyr. Han kastede nu og da et blik på hende med et lille smil. Han syntes, han så noget rørende uskyldigt i det forskræmte, sygelige lille ansigt.

Han fandt ikke embedsmanden eller hans kone, hvor han havde efterladt dem. Han gik rundt i mængden med hurtige skridt og mønstrede de forskellige ansigter, han mødte. Ufrivilligt lagde han mærke til en georgisk eller armensk familie bestående af en meget smuk gammel mand af orientalsk type iført en ny, stofbetrukket fåreskindskappe og nye støvler, en gammel kvinde af samme type og en ung kvinde. Denne meget unge kvinde syntes Pierre at være selve fuldkommenheden af orientalsk skønhed med sine skarpt tegnede, buede, sorte øjenbryn og den usædvanligt bløde, lysende farve i hendes lange, smukke, udtryksløse ansigt. Midt i de spredte ejendele og folkemængden på det åbne areal mindede hun i sin rige satinkappe med et klart lilla sjal over hovedet om en sart eksotisk plante kastet ud i sneen. Hun sad på nogle bylter lidt bag den gamle kvinde og kiggede under sine lange øjenvipper med ubevægelige, store, mandelformede øjne på jorden foran sig. Hun var tydeligvis bevidst om sin skønhed og ængstelig på grund af den. Hendes ansigt slog Pierre, og mens han skyndte sig langs hegnet, vendte han sig flere gange for at se på hende. Da han havde nået hegnet, stadig uden at have fundet dem, han søgte, standsede han og så sig omkring.
Med barnet i armene var hans skikkelse nu mere iøjnefaldende end før, og en gruppe russere, både mænd og kvinder, samlede sig om ham.
»Har De mistet nogen, min gode mand? De er vel selv af stand? Hvis barn er det?« spurgte de ham.
Pierre svarede, at barnet tilhørte en kvinde i en sort kappe, som havde siddet der med sine andre børn, og spurgte, om nogen vidste, hvor hun var gået hen.
»Det må jo være Anférov-familien,« sagde en gammel diakon til en koppearet bondekone. »Herren forbarm sig, Herren forbarm sig!« tilføjede han med sin sædvanlige bas.
»Anféroverne? Nej,« sagde kvinden. »De tog af sted om morgenen. Det må være Marja Nikolajevnas eller Ivánov-familiens!«
»Han siger 'en kvinde', og Marja Nikolajevna er en dame,« bemærkede en husslave.
»Kender De hende? Hun er mager og har lange tænder,« sagde Pierre.
»Det er Marja Nikolajevna! De gik ind i haven, da de her ulve styrtede ned over os,« sagde kvinden og pegede på de franske soldater.
»Å, Herre, forbarm Dig!« tilføjede diakonen.
»Gå derover, de er derovre. Det er hende! Hun blev ved med at jamre og græde,« fortsatte kvinden. »Det er hende. Herhen, den vej!«

Men Pierre lyttede ikke til kvinden. Han havde i nogle sekunder opmærksomt iagttaget, hvad der foregik få skridt derfra. Han så på den armenske familie og på to franske soldater, der var gået hen til dem. En af dem, en adræt lille mand, bar en blå frakke bundet om livet med et reb. Han havde en nathue på hovedet og var barfodet. Den anden, hvis udseende særligt slog Pierre, var en lang, mager, rundskuldret, lyshåret mand, langsom i sine bevægelser og med et idiotisk udtryk i ansigtet. Han bar en løs kvindekittel af vadmel, blå bukser og store iturevne hessiske støvler. Den lille barfodede franskmand i den blå frakke gik hen til armenierne og sagde noget, greb straks den gamle mand om benene, og den gamle mand begyndte øjeblikkeligt at trække sine støvler af. Den anden i vadmelskitlen standsede foran den smukke armenske pige og stod med hænderne i lommerne og stirrede ubevægeligt og tavst på hende.

»Her, tag barnet!« sagde Pierre bydende og hastigt til kvinden, idet han rakte hende den lille pige. »Giv hende tilbage til dem, giv hende tilbage!« næsten råbte han, satte barnet, der begyndte at skrige, på jorden og vendte sig atter mod franskmanden og den armenske familie.

Den gamle mand sad allerede barfodet. Den lille franskmand havde sikret sig hans anden støvle og slog den ene støvle mod den anden. Den gamle mand sagde noget med en stemme brudt af hulk, men Pierre fik kun et glimt af det; al hans opmærksomhed var rettet mod franskmanden i vadmelskitlen, som imens langsomt vuggende fra side til side var kommet nærmere den unge kvinde og med hænderne ude af lommerne havde grebet hende om halsen.
Den smukke armenske kvinde sad stadig ubevægeligt og i samme stilling med sine lange øjenvipper sænket, som om hun ikke så eller mærkede, hvad soldaten gjorde mod hende.

Mens Pierre løb de få skridt, der skilte ham fra franskmanden, var den høje plyndrer i vadmelskitlen allerede i færd med at rive halskæden af den unge armenske kvinde, og den unge kvinde greb sig til halsen med et gennemtrængende skrig.
»Lad den kvinde være!« udbrød Pierre hæst med rasende stemme, greb soldaten om de runde skuldre og kastede ham til side.
Soldaten faldt, rejste sig og løb sin vej. Men hans kammerat, der smed støvlerne og trak sin sabel, bevægede sig truende mod Pierre.
»Voyons, pas de bêtises!« råbte han.
»Hør nu her, ingen dumheder!«

Pierre var i et sådant anfald af raseri, at han ikke huskede noget, og hans kræfter tidobledes. Han styrtede mod den barfodede franskmand, og før denne nåede at trække sin sabel, slog han ham omkuld og hamrede løs med næverne. Bifaldende råb hørtes fra mængden omkring ham, og i samme øjeblik kom en bereden patrulje af franske ulaner til syne om hjørnet. Ulanerne red i trav hen til Pierre og franskmanden og omringede dem. Pierre huskede intet af, hvad der derefter skete. Han huskede kun, at han slog nogen, og at han selv blev slået, og til sidst mærkede han, at hans hænder var bundet, og at en flok franske soldater stod omkring ham og visiterede ham.
»Løjtnant, han har en dolk,« var de første ord, Pierre forstod.

»Ah, et våben?« sagde officeren og vendte sig mod den barfodede soldat, der var blevet arresteret sammen med Pierre. »Godt, det kan du fortælle alt om ved krigsretten.« Derpå vendte han sig mod Pierre. »Taler De fransk?«

Pierre så sig omkring med blodskudte øjne og svarede ikke. Hans ansigt har sandsynligvis set meget forfærdeligt ud, for officeren sagde noget hviskende, og fire ulaner mere forlod rækkerne og stillede sig på begge sider af Pierre.
»Taler De fransk?« spurgte officeren igen og holdt sig på afstand af Pierre. »Tilkald tolken.«
En lille mand i russisk civilt tøj red ud af rækkerne, og på hans klæder og måde at tale forstod Pierre øjeblikkeligt, at det var en fransk butikshandler fra en af Moskvas forretninger.
»Han ser ikke ud som en almindelig mand,« sagde tolken efter et grundigt blik på Pierre.
»Ah, han ligner i høj grad en brandstifter,« bemærkede officeren. »Og spørg ham, hvem han er,« tilføjede han.
»Hvem er De?« spurgte tolken på dårligt russisk. »De skal svare chefen.«
»Jeg vil ikke sige jer, hvem jeg er. Jeg er jeres fange — tag mig!« svarede Pierre pludselig på fransk.
»Ah, ah!« mumlede officeren med rynkede bryn. »Nå, march da!«
En mængde mennesker havde samlet sig om ulanerne. Nærmest Pierre stod den koppeartede bondekone med den lille pige, og da patruljen satte sig i bevægelse, trådte hun frem.
»Hvor tager I ham hen, den stakkels mand?« sagde hun. »Og den lille pige, den lille pige, hvad skal jeg gøre med hende, hvis det ikke er deres?« sagde kvinden.
»Hvad vil den kvinde?« spurgte officeren.
Pierre var som beruset. Hans begejstring voksede ved synet af den lille pige, han havde reddet.

»Hvad hun vil?« mumlede han. »Hun bringer mig min datter, som jeg netop har reddet fra flammerne,« sagde han. »Farvel!« Og uden at vide, hvordan denne formålsløse løgn var undsluppet ham, gik han med beslutsomme og triumferende skridt af sted mellem de franske soldater.

Den franske patrulje var en af dem, Durosnel havde sendt gennem Moskvas forskellige gader for at standse plyndringen og især for at pågribe brandstifterne, der ifølge den udbredte opfattelse, som den dag var opstået blandt de højere franske officerer, var skyld i ildebranden. Efter at have marcheret gennem flere gader arresterede patruljen fem russere mere, der var mistænkt: en lille handlende, to seminarister, en bonde og en husslave, foruden adskillige plyndrere. Men af alle disse mistænkte personer blev Pierre anset for den mest mistænkelige. Da de alle var bragt til overnatning i et stort hus ved Zúbov-volden, der blev brugt som vagtstation, blev Pierre anbragt for sig selv under streng bevogtning.

english.title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter 34
paragraphs: Pierre ran through various yards and side streets with his small burden and got back to the Gruzinski garden at the corner of the Povarskoy. At first he did not recognize the place he had set out from to look for the child. He could not, because it was now so crowded with people and with goods dragged out of the houses. Russian families had taken refuge there from the fire with their belongings, and among them were several French soldiers in assorted clothing. Pierre paid them no attention. He hurried to find the civil servant's family, so he could give the daughter back to her mother and go off to save someone else. Pierre felt he still had a great deal to do, and had to do it fast. He was flushed from the heat and the running, and at that moment he felt more strongly than ever the youth, vitality and resolve that had come over him when he ran to save the child. She had gone quiet now. She clung to Pierre's coat with her little hands and sat on his arm looking around her like a small wild animal. He glanced at her now and then with a faint smile. He thought he saw something touchingly innocent in that frightened, sickly little face.

He did not find the civil servant or his wife where he had left them. He walked quickly through the crowd, scanning the faces he passed. Without meaning to, he noticed a Georgian or Armenian family: a very handsome old man of Oriental type in a new, cloth-covered sheepskin coat and new boots, an old woman of the same type, and a young woman. To Pierre this young woman seemed the perfection of Oriental beauty. Her black eyebrows were sharply drawn and arched, and her long, lovely, expressionless face had an extraordinarily soft, bright color. Amid the scattered belongings and the crowd on the open ground, she wore a rich satin cloak and a bright lilac shawl on her head, and she looked like a delicate exotic plant thrown out onto the snow. She sat on some bundles a little behind the old woman. From under her long lashes she gazed at the ground in front of her with large, motionless, almond-shaped eyes. She was evidently aware of her beauty and afraid because of it. Her face struck Pierre, and as he hurried along the fence he turned several times to look at her. When he reached the fence and still had not found the people he was looking for, he stopped and looked around.
With the child in his arms he stood out more than before, and a group of Russians, men and women, gathered around him.
"Have you lost someone, my dear fellow? You're of the gentry yourself, aren't you? Whose child is it?" they asked him.
Pierre answered that the child belonged to a woman in a black coat who had been sitting there with her other children, and he asked whether anyone knew where she had gone.
"Why, that must be the Anferovs," said an old deacon, turning to a pockmarked peasant woman. "Lord have mercy, Lord have mercy!" he added in his usual bass.
"The Anferovs? No," said the woman. "They left in the morning. It must be Mary Nikolaevna's or the Ivanovs'!"
"He says 'a woman,' and Mary Nikolaevna is a lady," remarked a house serf.
"Do you know her? She's thin, with long teeth," said Pierre.
"That's Mary Nikolaevna! They went into the garden when these wolves swooped down," said the woman, pointing at the French soldiers.
"O Lord, have mercy!" added the deacon.
"Go over that way, they're there. It's her! She kept on wailing and crying," the woman went on. "It's her. Here, this way!"

But Pierre was not listening to the woman. For some seconds he had been watching intently something that was happening a few steps away. He was looking at the Armenian family and at two French soldiers who had walked up to them. One of them was a nimble little man in a blue coat tied around the waist with a rope. He had a nightcap on his head, and his feet were bare. The other struck Pierre especially. He was a tall, lank, round-shouldered, fair-haired man, slow in his movements, with an idiotic look on his face. He wore a woman's loose frieze gown, blue trousers and big torn Hessian boots. The little barefoot Frenchman in the blue coat went up to the Armenians, said something and at once seized the old man by the legs, and the old man immediately began pulling off his boots. The other, in the frieze gown, stopped in front of the beautiful Armenian girl and stood staring at her, motionless and silent, with his hands in his pockets.

"Here, take the child!" Pierre said to the woman, sharply and in a hurry, handing the little girl to her. "Give her back to them, give her back!" he almost shouted. He set the child, who began to scream, on the ground and looked again at the Frenchman and the Armenian family.

The old man was already sitting barefoot. The little Frenchman had got his second boot and was slapping the two boots together. The old man was saying something in a voice broken by sobs, but Pierre barely caught a glimpse of this. All his attention was on the Frenchman in the frieze gown, who by now had swayed slowly over to the young woman. He took his hands out of his pockets and seized her by the neck.
The beautiful Armenian was still sitting motionless in the same posture, her long lashes lowered, as if she neither saw nor felt what the soldier was doing to her.

Pierre ran the few steps that separated him from the Frenchman. By then the tall marauder in the frieze gown was already tearing off the necklace the young Armenian wore, and the young woman, clutching at her neck, screamed piercingly.
"Leave that woman alone!" Pierre shouted hoarsely in a furious voice. He seized the soldier by his round shoulders and threw him aside.
The soldier fell, got up and ran away. But his comrade threw down the boots, drew his sword and moved threateningly toward Pierre.
"Voyons, pas de bêtises!" * he cried.
* "Look here, no nonsense!"

Pierre was in such a transport of rage that he remembered nothing, and his strength grew tenfold. He rushed at the barefoot Frenchman and, before the man had time to draw his sword, knocked him off his feet and pounded him with his fists. Cries of approval came from the crowd around them. At the same moment a mounted patrol of French Uhlans appeared around the corner. The Uhlans trotted up to Pierre and the Frenchman and surrounded them. Pierre remembered nothing of what happened next. He only remembered beating someone and being beaten, and finally feeling that his hands were tied and that a crowd of French soldiers stood around him searching him.
"Lieutenant, he has a dagger," were the first words Pierre understood.

"Ah, a weapon?" said the officer, and he turned to the barefoot soldier who had been arrested with Pierre. "All right, you can tell all about it at the court-martial." Then he turned to Pierre. "Do you speak French?"

Pierre looked around him with bloodshot eyes and did not answer. His face probably looked terrible, because the officer whispered something, and four more Uhlans left the ranks and placed themselves on either side of Pierre.
"Do you speak French?" the officer asked again, keeping away from Pierre. "Call the interpreter."
A little man in Russian civilian clothes rode out of the ranks. From his clothes and his way of speaking, Pierre knew at once that he was a French salesman from one of the Moscow shops.
"He doesn't look like a common man," said the interpreter, after a searching look at Pierre.
"Ah, he looks very much like an incendiary," remarked the officer. "And ask him who he is," he added.
"Who are you?" asked the interpreter in poor Russian. "You must answer the chief."
"I won't tell you who I am. I am your prisoner — take me!" Pierre suddenly answered in French.
"Ah, ah!" the officer muttered with a frown. "Well then, march!"
A crowd had gathered around the Uhlans. The pockmarked peasant woman with the little girl stood nearest to Pierre, and when the patrol set off she stepped forward.
"Where are they taking you, you poor dear?" she said. "And the little girl, the little girl, what am I to do with her if she's not theirs?" said the woman.
"What does that woman want?" asked the officer.
Pierre felt as if he were drunk. The sight of the little girl he had saved made his elation even greater.

"What does she want?" he murmured. "She's bringing me my daughter, whom I have just saved from the flames," he said. "Good-by!" He had no idea how this pointless lie had slipped out of him. He went along between the French soldiers with resolute, triumphant steps.

The French patrol was one of those that Durosnel had ordered into the various streets of Moscow to put a stop to the pillaging and, above all, to catch the incendiaries. The general opinion among the higher French officers, formed that very day, held that the incendiaries were the cause of the fires. After marching through a number of streets, the patrol arrested five more Russian suspects: a small shopkeeper, two seminary students, a peasant and a house serf, besides several looters. But of all these suspects, Pierre was considered the most suspicious. They were all brought for the night to a large house on the Zubov Rampart that was being used as a guardhouse, and there Pierre was put apart under strict guard.
